summary: This document describes how signaling intermediaries, often called Session Border Controllers, behave when performing Hosted NAT Traversal for real-time media. It covers media relaying and latching, which let devices behind NATs communicate. It is non-normative.

eli5.summary: Devices behind home routers cannot be reached directly. A helper in the middle notices where the first packets come from and then sends replies back there. This RFC describes that trick.

questions: what is a session border controller
subtitle: How session border controllers learn where a NATed phone really is by watching where its first media packets come from.

tldr.problem: SIP and similar protocols put private addresses and ports inside session descriptions, which are unusable across NATs, and NATs block incoming packets until the device sends first.
tldr.mechanism: A signaling intermediary (SBC) rewrites the addresses to point at its media relay, then latches onto the source address and port of the first media packets it receives and sends return media there.
tldr.outcome: The RFC documents existing practice but advises against latching over the Internet unless its security issues are solved, and recommends ICE and TURN instead.

facts.label: Latching scope
facts.value: Usually once per peer until a new offer and answer

facts.label: Required of the NATed UA
facts.value: Symmetric RTP, able to send first

today: RFC 7362 is an Informational document and is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC. It advises against using latching over the Internet unless all its security considerations are solved, and recommends ICE and TURN instead.

sections.title: Why Hosted NAT Traversal Exists
sections.content:
This RFC is non-normative. It describes what signaling intermediaries, often called Session Border Controllers (SBCs), do when performing Hosted NAT Traversal (HNT). HNT uses media relaying and latching so devices behind NATs can talk to each other.

SIP and similar protocols carry IP addresses and ports in bodies such as SDP. Those are unusable unless every peer is behind the same NAT. STUN, TURN and ICE did not exist when SIP deployment started, and early STUN was unreliable, so SBCs began using proprietary mechanisms, usually transparent to endpoints.

The text says a vast majority of SIP domains used HNT at publication time despite ICE. It does not argue that HNT is better than ICE.
sections.eli5: Phones behind home routers write down their private room numbers, which nobody outside can use. A helper at the front desk was invented to sort that out.

sections.title: The NAT Problems and Signaling Impact
sections.content:
Three problems are listed. Addresses in SDP are private, not the ones the NAT maps to. NATs and firewalls drop packets from outside until the device sends out first. Some NATs filter by endpoint, so a device may only receive from the same remote IP and port it sends to.

To handle this, the SBC sits on the public side and rewrites signaling so peers are given the address of a media relay it controls. The relay is typically co-located with the SBC, uses the same IP address family as signaling, and gets port numbers allocated dynamically in an implementation-specific way.

Under the offer/answer model, an SBC may still hold back media. For example, it may wait for a SIP 200 response before sending, to prevent toll fraud.
sections.eli5: The front desk tells each guest the desk's own number instead of their private room number, so calls always come to the desk first.

sections.title: How Latching Works
sections.content:
The UA behind the NAT advertises its private address:port, so the SBC cannot yet know the public mapping. The relay therefore waits and latches.

  1. On Alice's offer, the SBC allocates relay address:port tuples and advertises them to Bob.
  2. When Bob answers, it allocates a second set and puts it in the answer to Alice.
  3. The relay receives packets on the allocated ports and uses their source address:port as the destination for media going the other way.
  4. Alice's source is her NAT's public mapping, so replies find their way to her. Bob's source is latched the same way.

Latching is usually done once per peer and not allowed to change until a new offer and answer. A sudden port change may indicate session hijack, though a NAT re-mapping can also cause it, so advanced SBCs allow some flexibility.

The UA must use symmetric RTP (same ports to send and listen) and must be able to send first. If two HNT servers each wait for the other, a deadlock can occur, so relays often start streaming to the offered address before receiving traffic. Many SBCs also support TCP latching, which forces the NATed UA to be the TCP client and may splice connections.
sections.eli5: The helper waits for your first shout, sees which window it came from, and then always throws the answer back to that window.

sections.title: Caveats of Relaying
sections.content:
HNT and latching are generally found to work reliably, but with caveats. UAs are not aware it is happening, so it cannot be combined with ICE, which tries several traversal techniques. Rewriting address information may even prevent ICE through its ice-mismatch rules.

Media also goes through a relay instead of the direct path, with reduced scalability and increased latency. SBC administrators see this as a benefit: they can check that media flows, assess quality and learn why it failed, and operator relays may use paths optimized for media.
sections.eli5: Sending every message through the front desk is slower, but the desk can check that every message arrived.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An SBC may latch onto a wrong or malicious source. ICE provides authentication tokens (ice-ufrag and ice-pwd) to confirm a peer first; latching has no such check. A malicious source could flood the SBC's latching UDP ports to stop calls from succeeding.

The common defense is restricted latching: only latch to packets from the same public IP address the SIP UA uses for signaling. Attackers who know that IP can still spoof it, but then only that IP's media is hurt. An attacker behind the same NAT, which is a particular concern with Carrier-Grade NATs, can still be latched to and receive the media.

The RFC says SRTP should be used independently of HNT, and that failing to use it is a serious threat for users behind Carrier-Grade NATs and is considered a harmful practice. Because the SBC modifies SDP, S/MIME and SIP Identity signing cannot be used unless the SBC re-signs.
sections.eli5: A stranger standing next to you could shout first and trick the helper into sending your answers to them. Checking who is shouting, and sealing the messages, helps.
